title: Review: 2XO The Hip-Hop Blend Bourbon
summary:
Dixon Dedman has become one of the most recognizable names in American whiskey, first gaining a following through his early releases of Kentucky Owl. After a seven-year run with the brand, Dedman departed in 2021. In November 2022, he launched 2XO, short for Two Times Oak, with The Phoenix Blend serving as the debut release.…

The post Review: 2XO The Hip-Hop Blend Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Dixon Dedman has become one of the most recognizable names in American whiskey, first gaining a following through his early releases of Kentucky Owl. After a seven-year run with the brand, Dedman departed in 2021. In November 2022, he launched 2XO, short for Two Times Oak, with The Phoenix Blend serving as the debut release.

In 2026, Dedman unveiled the seventh installment in the 2XO Collectible Series, The Hip-Hop Blend. As the name suggests, the bourbon pays tribute to “Rapper’s Delight,” the 1979 single by the Sugarhill Gang. Released by Sugar Hill Records, the song became the first rap single to reach the Top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100 and helped establish rap as a force in mainstream music. The Hip-Hop Blend takes its inspiration from that milestone, bringing bourbon and hip-hop together in a rather literal fashion.

For anyone who has spent time with “Rapper’s Delight,” the connection is hard to miss. The song opens with “I said a hip hop,” and Dedman’s latest release takes that phrase as a cue for a bourbon built around multiple components, multiple barrel treatments and two bourbon mashbills.

The Hip-Hop Blend is made from two different bourbon mashbills, although the finished blend actually consists of four separate components. Roughly 10% is a low-rye bourbon made from a mashbill of 74% corn, 18% rye and 8% malted barley. It was distilled by an undisclosed heritage distillery in Kentucky that has been making whiskey for Dedman since 2017.

Barton 1792 is known for using a 74% corn, 18% rye and 8% malted barley mashbill, but Dedman did not confirm whether Barton 1792 distilled this portion of The Hip-Hop Blend.

The remaining 90% comes from a high-rye bourbon made from 60% corn, 35% rye and 5% malted barley. This whiskey has been distilled for Dedman by a heritage distillery in Kentucky since 2015. Dedman was clear on one point: Four Roses did not distill this component.

That 90% portion consists of three separate lots, each representing 30% of the finished blend. The lots are similar in age, though not identical, and all underwent secondary maturation in new charred oak barrels. The high-rye bourbon came off the still at 120 proof before entering its initial barrels at 118 proof.

Maturation took place either on the lower levels of Dedman’s contracted aging facilities or in a palletized storage facility. As a result, the bourbon’s proof declined during maturation.

Looking at the finished blend, the 10% low-rye component is aged between 6.5 and 7 years. Lot A accounts for 30% of the blend and is 8 years old. It underwent secondary maturation in a new charred barrel from Independent Stave Co. with a #4 char. Lot B also accounts for 30% of the blend and is 7 years old, with secondary maturation in a new charred Independent Stave Co. barrel with a #3 char. Lot C makes up the final 30% and is also 7 years old, spending secondary maturation in a new charred Independent Stave Co. barrel with a #4 char.

Every bourbon used for secondary maturation was at least 6 years old before entering the new barrels, and each spent at least one calendar year in the new charred oak barrels supplied by Independent Stave Company.

All blending took place after secondary maturation. The resulting bourbon came together at a natural harvest proof of 111.

There is a certain poetry to the concept. “Rapper’s Delight” took several different musical elements and turned them into something that helped define an entirely new era of popular music. The Hip-Hop Blend takes several bourbon lots, two mashbills and two stages of barrel maturation and brings them together under the 2XO name.

But the real question remains: Is Dixon Dedman’s newest blend an appropriate tribute to “Rapper’s Delight,” and will it prove to be an equal delight for bourbon lovers? Should bourbon drinkers jump on it?

2Xo The Hip-Hop Blend Kentucky Bourbon Review

The nose opens with dried orange peel and dark brown sugar before giving way to heavily toasted coconut, though the coconut eventually comes across as more charred than toasted. Cinnamon arrives later, soft and powdery, much like the cinnamon dusting on Hostess Donettes, followed by toasted pecans. The nose is certainly a delight.

The palate leads with dense chocolate fudge and buttery toffee. Beeswax and homemade cinnamon toast arrive through the mid-palate. This is not the artificial Cinnamon Toast Crunch note that often appears in bourbon that has spent time in amburana wood. Instead, the cinnamon toast comes across as natural and far less potent.

The mouthfeel is quite oily, while the spice picks up on the finish. It begins with chai spice before transitioning to flaky vanilla wafers and toasted coconut.

From the first sip to the last, it is clear that Dixon Dedman has not lost his touch. The Hip-Hop Blend delivers at every point, making good on the promise of its name and serving as a fitting bourbon tribute to “Rapper’s Delight.” This one gets the job done, and for bourbon lovers given the opportunity, jumping on it makes sense.

104 proof.

A / $90

title: Review: 3 Wines from the Maison Vernhes Alliance Wine Collective
summary:
The premise behind Maison Vernhes Alliance (MVA), stripped of marketing gloss, is simple enough and should ring familiar to loyal readers: it’s a wine collective built entirely around the premise that small European producers are out there making genuinely great wine but simply cannot be bothered or, more accurately, cannot afford, to fight their way…

The post Review: 3 Wines from the Maison Vernhes Alliance Wine Collective appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The premise behind Maison Vernhes Alliance (MVA), stripped of marketing gloss, is simple enough and should ring familiar to loyal readers: it’s a wine collective built entirely around the premise that small European producers are out there making genuinely great wine but simply cannot be bothered or, more accurately, cannot afford, to fight their way into the retail shelf-space wars that larger houses win through sheer financial attrition.

So MVA finds them directly, cuts out the part of the industry where a wine has to survive three middlemen and a distributor’s opinions before it reaches you, and builds a subscription around the whole operation. Every two months, six bottles show up, curated loosely around whatever preferences you’ve indicated, at a price landing somewhere between $30 and $35 a bottle depending on your tier. Either way, it’s a reasonable fee for small producer wines from Europe, or the right amount of money necessary to never again endure small talk with the guy at your local wine shop who has Passionate Opinions about wine and will share them whether you asked or not.

The wines are sourced from some of Europe’s most esteemed regions, with a few detours into places that don’t immediately show up on a wine lover’s map. The whole model is a passport arriving in a cardboard box in front of your Ring camera instead of requiring air travel, lost luggage and people on a plane using the speakerphone setting. We were fortunate to receive a sampling from their latest collection: three reds, delivered right in time for National Red Wine Day.

2021 Chateau Les Coriselle Calcaire – Leading off things nicely: a Malbec from Cahors. It bears more than a passing resemblance to its distant cousins from Argentina, with earthy notes of black currant and pepper set against savory spice. A touch of chocolate enters and exits the conversation on the palate quickly, diminished against the ever-present black currant. The finish is the real treat, with a blend of ripe plum and nutmeg lingering about as it all recedes. Very drinkable and ready for autumn. A- / $41

2020 Chateau Pech Redon L’Epervier – The density of this 50/50 Syrah Mourvèdre blend pours dense and earthy, requiring about 30 minutes or so to sort itself out. However, that big quality quickly fades and a blend of dark cherry and elderberry becomes the main theme running throughout. Layers of licorice, graphite and cracked pepper weave in and out on the palate. Once the sheer density out of the bottle wears away, the opulence comes through, revealing a wine that doesn’t run short on complexity.  B+ / $42

2021 Manzone La Marchesa Barbera d’Alba Superiore DOC – Dense and rich with fulsome notes of cherry and blackberry up front and baking spices lingering well into the finish. A bit of tobacco leaf and black tea give it an earthy kick on the finish, putting the berry compote on the palate firmly in balance. Ignore the food pairing and save this for the campfire.  B+ / $42

If these reds are indicative of the quality found throughout, this very well may be something worth investigating as a holiday present for the introverted wine lovers in your life.

title: Review: Chicken Cock Old Glory
summary:
Chicken Cock has dropped a few out-there releases since its re-inception in 2017 as a premium whiskey producer, but none of them are as unique, I think, as Chicken Cock Old Glory. What’s in the bottle? A blend of 70% Chicken Cock Kentucky Straight Rye Whiskey with 30% Laird’s Apple Brandy — an homage to…

The post Review: Chicken Cock Old Glory appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Chicken Cock has dropped a few out-there releases since its re-inception in 2017 as a premium whiskey producer, but none of them are as unique, I think, as Chicken Cock Old Glory. What’s in the bottle? A blend of 70% Chicken Cock Kentucky Straight Rye Whiskey with 30% Laird’s Apple Brandy — an homage to two of America’s ancestral spirits. This was dropped for the big U.S. 250th anniversary last month but it slipped through the cracks here until now.

Both components are aged a minimum of 4 years, which is young for rye and extremely young for apple brandy. Let’s salute the flag and give it a taste.

Chicken Cock Old Glory Review

There’s definitely a caramel apple element on the nose here, though it isn’t as distinct as you might expect, buried under significant florals, largely dried and potpourri-like, with overtones of baby’s breath and, eventually, some buttery honeysuckle.

The palate is, perhaps unsurprisingly given the components, extremely dry — almost dusty on first blush, before it gets some air in it. Here the blend shows off significant astringency, again evoking dried white flowers plus lavender and fresh linens, some of the hallmarks of young brandy, whether grape or otherwise. Time spent with Old Glory is rewarding, the spirit settling into slightly sweeter territory — and becoming more evocative of apples — albeit never wandering far from the flower shop. Hints of green peppercorn, saffron, and dusky hemp cling to the midpalate, coating the tongue.

The finish is, admittedly, a little harsh, and it never really settles down the way I hoped it would, even after time in glass and through the addition of water, which serves merely to dull the overall experience. I love a great rye and a great apple brandy, but this blend is just too young to get anything meaningful going. At $65, it’s a bit of a tough sell.

100 proof.

B- / $65

title: Review: Tequila Partida High-Proof Single Barrel Reposado – Barrels 7, 12, and 17
summary:
Partida launched a single barrel program in 2020, rolling out a collection of barrels of its reposado. 30 barrels in total were offered in three different styles (we just tasted one) — but notably all were bottled at 80 proof. This year, Partida expands on that concept with the release of 20 more barrels of…

The post Review: Tequila Partida High-Proof Single Barrel Reposado – Barrels 7, 12, and 17 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Partida launched a single barrel program in 2020, rolling out a collection of barrels of its reposado. 30 barrels in total were offered in three different styles (we just tasted one) — but notably all were bottled at 80 proof.

This year, Partida expands on that concept with the release of 20 more barrels of reposado, only this time the outfit is dropping them at higher proof. The twist: The purchaser of the bottles gets to pick the proof, so retailers and bars can tailor the alcohol to their clientele’s preference, between 90 and 110 proof. Purchasers can select barrels on site in Jalisco or by sampling a tasting kit of three offerings (which is what we were able to do in preparing this review).

As is standard for Partida, these barrels are aged a minimum of six months in custom-toasted, single-use ex-bourbon barrels. Our samples were bottled at 54% abv. Obviously pricing will vary based on the seller and the proof point they choose for their barrel, but SRPs begin at $49.

Here’s a look at how the three barrels we were able to sample compare and contrast. Each 108 proof.

Tequila Partida High-Proof Single Barrel Reposado Barrel 7 Review

Peppery and full of spice, this is one of the racier reposados I’ve tasted of late, bursting with green pepper and jalapeno notes on both nose and palate. There’s a moderating sweetness here that keeps the spice — and the heat — in check, though the finish is rather lemony and and bright, almost acidic, with a moderate amount of salt to back it up. A powerhouse that drinks more like a blanco. A-

Tequila Partida High-Proof Single Barrel Reposado Barrel 12 Review

With considerably less spice on display here, this tequila amps up its citrus notes, lemon dominant alongside a gentler layer of lime leaf and rind. While it’s not overwhelming with those jalapeno notes, it does leave a bit of a scorching wake thanks to the heat from the higher abv, the finish evoking white pepper and cinnamon. A gentle milk chocolate quality builds with time in glass, making this quite a versatile crowd-pleaser with more of a traditionally authentic reposado quality. A-

Tequila Partida High-Proof Single Barrel Reposado Barrel 17 Review

A cousin to Barrel 7, this expression returns to spicier climes, though it’s amply tempered by lemon peel and even a touch of grapefruit, making this solid Paloma fodder. The finish is more soothing than Barrel 7, however, with vanilla and chocolate slowly creeping into the picture, considerably tempering the upfront heat. The abv is also less overtly evident here than in the other two tequilas, a creamy texture offering silky overtones of coconut layered across the moderately lengthy (and perfectly balanced) finish. A

each $49 and up

title: Review: Andalusia Stryker Madeira Cask American Single Malt
summary:
On January 19, 2025, the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau officially recognized American single malt whiskey as a category of American whiskey. That designation may be new, but American single malt whiskey is not. American distillers had been developing their own approach to malt whiskey for years before the category received official recognition.…

The post Review: Andalusia Stryker Madeira Cask American Single Malt appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
On January 19, 2025, the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau officially recognized American single malt whiskey as a category of American whiskey. That designation may be new, but American single malt whiskey is not. American distillers had been developing their own approach to malt whiskey for years before the category received official recognition.

For many whiskey drinkers around the world, the words “single malt” tend to point immediately toward Scotland, and often toward the peated single malts of Islay. But peat smoke is not inherently synonymous with single malt. Much of that association comes from Scottish history.

Thousands of years ago, Scotland was considerably more heavily forested than it is today. Forests were cleared for agriculture, grazing, construction, shipbuilding, charcoal, and fuel. By the time Scotch whisky production was becoming established, wood was no longer an endlessly available fuel source in many parts of the country. Peat, however, was readily available. Scotland’s extensive peat bogs provided a local source of fuel, and peat became an important part of everyday life, including the malting of barley.

Malting requires heat to stop germination and dry the grain. Historically, burning peat was a practical way to generate that heat. The smoke inevitably became part of the malt and, eventually, part of the identity of certain Scotch whiskies.

Tradition has a funny way of turning necessity into identity.

American single malt whiskey does not have to follow that same path. American distillers certainly use peat, and some do, but the category also gives them an opportunity to ask a different question: What does malt whiskey taste like when it is allowed to express an American sense of place?

That can mean different fuels, different woods, different maturation environments, and different approaches to creating smoke and shaping the malt profile. The objective is not necessarily to make American Scotch. It is to make American single malt.

Located in Blanco, Texas, Andalusia Whiskey Company makes American single malt that is proudly Texas. In 2026, the Blanco distillery released a 116 proof expression of Andalusia Stryker Madeira Cask American Single Malt.

The mashbill consists of 100% malted barley, primarily pale 2-row from Great Western Malting, along with a small percentage of Dark Chocolate and Munich malt grown and malted in Wildorado, Texas, by Maverick Malthouse. While the mashbill is entirely malted barley, there is plenty going on within that 100%.

Ninety percent of the malted barley is unsmoked, while 10% is smoked. The smoked portion can be broken down further: 70% is smoked with oak, 20% with applewood, and 10% with mesquite. No peat smoke.

The grain was fermented for seven days in a closed-top, 2,000-gallon fermenter using a basic malt whiskey yeast, with the temperature maintained between 85 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit. The mash was triple-distilled on a copper pot still, with the spirit coming off the still at an aggregate proof of roughly 145. It then entered new, charred oak barrels with a No. 3 char from Kelvin Cooperage at between 117 and 120 proof.

After at least three years of primary maturation, the casks were selected and blended before being transferred into three 220-liter Madeira casks. The Madeira casks typically rest in a lower section of the hottest area of the rickhouse for a minimum of three months. For this particular batch, however, the whiskey spent just shy of a full year in Madeira casks, entering them at 120.5 proof.

Andalusia Whiskey Company puts an unmistakably American and Texas spin on single malt, with a whiskey that clearly does not aim to be Scotch.

Is an approach like this worthy of changing how the world thinks about single malt? Let’s find out.

Andalusia Stryker Madeira Cask Finished American Single Malt Whiskey Review

Right out of the gate, the smoke is apparent, with smoldering sage taking over the nose. The smoke doesn’t stop there, as heavily smoked bacon quickly joins the mix. Dense pound cake develops before the smoke surfaces again in the form of charred plums, with dark chocolate rounding out the bouquet.

It’s fascinating that only 10% of the barley is smoked, particularly given how many different expressions of smoke show up on the nose. This is never simply one smoky note. There are several discernible smoky notes, brought about by three different types of smoke working together.

The palate opens with an extremely brief hit of cranberry juice before instantly flipping to mesquite smoke. It’s very noticeable, yet nowhere near overwhelming. Mingling with the mesquite is a medicinal cherry cough drop, followed by stewed green apples and cacao as the mid-palate develops.

The smoky profile is just right, and the smoke adds a tremendous amount of body to the whiskey, creating an exceptionally chewy mouthfeel. I’m not sure I’ve ever experienced an American single malt with this much chewiness on the palate.

The finish ushers in smoked sea salt and slightly scorched grenadine, along with more red fruit in the form of dehydrated strawberries. The combination creates a sensation much like Kellogg’s Special K Red Berries breakfast cereal before tobacco brings everything to a close.

This is quite the powerhouse of an American single malt whiskey. Admittedly, I don’t typically care for peated Scotch, but the smoky profile here unexpectedly works for me in a big way. For those who enjoy smoky whiskey, this is wildly enticing. For those who typically avoid smoky whiskey, this is one that could make them reconsider that stance.

This is arguably among my Top 10 American single malt whiskies that I’ve tried. I also haven’t been able to try anything from Still Austin in a few years. The last Still Austin expression I tasted was the flagship cask strength bourbon aged for two years, so I’ve missed out on the more recent, heavily hyped releases from Still Austin. I understand the cult following, but this release from Andalusia Whiskey Co. is the best Texas-distilled whiskey I’ve personally experienced to date.

116 proof.

A / $65

title: Review: Bardstown Bourbon Co. Victoria Pineapple Barrel Finish
summary:
If you haven’t been paying close attention, you might have missed the fact that Bardstown Bourbon Co. has become one of the most innovative distilleries in America, turning out one unusual whiskey after another, relying either on unexpected blends or out-there finishes. Its latest release, Victoria Pineapple, is one of the latter, a 10 year old…

The post Review: Bardstown Bourbon Co. Victoria Pineapple Barrel Finish appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
If you haven’t been paying close attention, you might have missed the fact that Bardstown Bourbon Co. has become one of the most innovative distilleries in America, turning out one unusual whiskey after another, relying either on unexpected blends or out-there finishes. Its latest release, Victoria Pineapple, is one of the latter, a 10 year old blend of bourbon and rye that features a massive 27 month finishing time in rum barrels “refined with fresh pineapple and additional wood staves.”

The fine print on the side of the label reveals the breakdown of the component whiskeys: 40% 11 year old  bourbon with a 75% corn, 21% rye, 4% barley mash; 40% 10 year old bourbon with the same mash; and 20% 10 year old rye with the classic 95% rye, 5% barley recipe. All is distilled in Indiana, presumably at MGP.

As for the finishing: “The rum that previously occupied these casks has earned a devoted following among bartenders and spirits enthusiasts, due to its distinctive production process, in which prized Victoria pineapples are incorporated directly during maturation. Intrigued by the remarkable tropical character those casks produced, Bardstown Bourbon Company set out to honor the process, rather than simply use the barrels as finishing vessels.”

Label design is courtesy of multimedia artist Margaret Archambault.

We were lucky to get a bottle of this new release for review after tasting it in New Orleans at Tales of the Cocktail with master blender Dan Callaway. Here’s our full review after having had ample time to sit with it.

Bardstown Bourbon Co. Victoria Pineapple Barrel Finish Review

Pouring a golden brown, the whiskey immediately evokes on the nose exactly what you think: pineapple, big and sweet, but with an oxidized note that gives it some real gravity. Aromas of oloroso sherry, pitted cherries, and smoldering oak emerge with time in glass, eventually leading to a somewhat leathery character, bathed in overtones of floral incense.

Pineapple again leads the way on the palate, this time well caramelized, hinting at mango and some banana, again flambeed. The body is bold at 53% abv, with a sweet Orange Julius character that gives the intense fruit some rich and lively creaminess. The fruit bomb continues to the finish, where caramel and some chocolate notes finally emerge, followed again by a reprise of fresh, juicy pineapple.

Callaway says that his goal was never to make whiskey taste like pineapple, but it’s hard to say that isn’t exactly what happened here — and in the best possible way. Rarely have I encountered a whiskey that comes across as so incredibly delightful and effusive — and hard to put down. Some may see this as a gimmick, but, jeez, what a gimmick it is.

106 pro0f.

A / $140

title: Review: Little Book Blended Whiskey Chapter 10: “All the Wiser” (2026)
summary:
Freddie Noe’s Little Book celebrates a milestone this season with its 10th release: “All the Wiser,” a name which nods at the lessons learned over a decade of Little Book releases: Chapter 10 doesn’t just celebrate a decade of boundary-pushing blending but captures the evolution of one of American whiskey’s most innovative makers. Since its…

The post Review: Little Book Blended Whiskey Chapter 10: “All the Wiser” (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Freddie Noe’s Little Book celebrates a milestone this season with its 10th release: “All the Wiser,” a name which nods at the lessons learned over a decade of Little Book releases:

Chapter 10 doesn’t just celebrate a decade of boundary-pushing blending but captures the evolution of one of American whiskey’s most innovative makers.

Since its inception, Little Book has been Freddie’s personal playground: an annual series that honors his grandfather Booker’s fearless approach to whiskey while carving out a distinctly modern perspective. But Chapter 10 is different. It’s not just another installment; it’s the culmination of everything Freddie has learned along the way.

After years of chasing precision and “perfect” blends, Freddie shifted his philosophy for this release. “All The Wiser” reflects a more intuitive approach, one that embraces the unpredictability of blending and allows the whiskey itself to lead. The result is a whiskey that feels more discovered than past releases.

This year’s blend draws from a spectrum of aged expressions across The James B. Beam Distilling Co. portfolio, including components finished in sherry and toasted bourbon casks.

It’s kind of buried in the prose, but the big change here is that this expression is composed of a kind of “greatest hits” of other (finished) Beam releases rather than pulling from unblended barrels scattered around the rickhouses. Here’s the rundown of what’s in the blend:

  • 14 year old Basil Hayden
  • 11 year old Knob Creek
  • 10 year old Booker’s
  • 9 year old Knob Creek
  • 9 year old Baker’s
  • 4 year old Jim Beam finished in sherry and toasted bourbon casks

Proportions, as usual, are not disclosed. Note that while all the components are bourbons, the finished product is officially being sold as a “blended straight whiskey.”

Little Book Blended Whiskey Chapter 10: “All the Wiser” (2026) Review

An aggressive tea leaf quality dominates the nose upon pouring, lightly sweetened black tea with overtones of clove and nutmeg. Time in glass allows a fruitier element of fig jam to emerge, sparring curiously with gentler notes of black coffee that smolder on the back end.

The palate is a scorcher at full strength. Water is helpful in taming the heat and coaxing out more nuance. What struck me most clearly on the tongue was the whiskey’s dense sweetness, with sweet nougat leading to notes of walnut and chestnut, both glazed in brown sugar. A fruitcake character builds from there as those clove and nutmeg elements find a friend in a healthy punch of cinnamon, with a touch of orange peel grated over the top. The whiskey isn’t especially woody until the conclusion, which has a lightly resinous character that evokes polished oak and eucalyptus, a pinch of mint leading the way out of a delightful, well-balanced experience.

122.6 proof.

A- / $160 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Wines of Opolo, 2026 Releases
summary:
Opolo‘s 2026 releases have started arriving, and we’re tucking into five offerings from this Paso Robles operation — surely with more to come as the year stretches on. Let’s dive in. 2023 Opolo Rhapsody Willow Creek District – Designed as a Left Bank style Bordeaux, heavy on Cabernet Sauvignon and blended with Petit Verdot, Malbec,…

The post Review: Wines of Opolo, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Opolo‘s 2026 releases have started arriving, and we’re tucking into five offerings from this Paso Robles operation — surely with more to come as the year stretches on. Let’s dive in.

2023 Opolo Rhapsody Willow Creek District – Designed as a Left Bank style Bordeaux, heavy on Cabernet Sauvignon and blended with Petit Verdot, Malbec, Merlot, and Cabernet Franc. Soft and distant at first blush but increasingly approachable as it develops in glass, an initially doughy character giving way to layered currant and blueberry notes, followed by some earthier elements, first clove, then anise, then dark chocolate. Still quite tannic on the finish, my expectation is that this wine will develop as it ages in cellar to more fully realize its fruitier side. Even now it is drinking with a lively approachability, and a quick decanting can quickly get it up to speed. A- / $60

2023 Opolo Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve Collection Willow Creek District – Initially dense with currants and cherry notes, this hefty cab soon opens up to showcase brighter fruit — particularly juicy orange plus flowery blossoms, layered with vanilla and milk chocolate. The tannin structure has developed well here already, giving the wine an edge of rhubarb and a light anise quality, leading to a darker, more acidic orange-chocolate character on the finish, with touches of earthy graphite lingering. While I’d normally say a wine like this demands a heavy steak dinner as a companion, I paired it with pan-roasted salmon, and it acquitted itself just fine. A few more years in cellar may help develop things further, however. A- / $50

2023 Opolo Willow Cuvee Reserve Collection Willow Creek District – Opolo’s Right Bank wine, predominantly Merlot, plus Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, and Petit Verdot. Dense and jammy, this is a brazenly fruit-forward wine that melds extracted plums and currants with bittersweet chocolate. Plenty of vanilla in syrup give the wine an exuberant sweetness, though time in glass helps everything to settle into a more spice-forward groove. Touches of anise and cinnamon emerge on the finish, and although it’s not nearly as complex as the Rhapsody bottling, it still acquits itself admirably. B+ / $50

2023 Opolo Cabernet Sauvignon Paso Robles – A slightly jammier version of the Reserve cabernet, this expression is massive with currants and blackberries before delving into notes of chocolate and vanilla. The more citrus-forward fruit of the Reserve Collection wine is almost absent here, save for a hint of orange peel that lingers on the finish, but otherwise this acquits itself as a simpler but wholly approachable wine, ready for by-the-glass service for those who want a more decadent aperitif to get them prepped for a night of prime rib. Certainly a more than solid option given the price. B+ / $42

2024 Opolo Merlot Summit Creek – The only miss in this lineup, this merlot is blown out with extracted fruit, dense with Hershey’s syrup poured over raspberries and currants. Coffee notes build on the dense, unctuous finish, with layers of toasted coconut at times making the wine approach the flavors of an underbaked Black Forest cake. B- / $22

title: Review: Hibiki 12 Years Old (Updated 2026)
summary:

content:
Suntory’s Hibiki 12 Years Old got its first U.S. release in 2009, and the expression has been on and off the market ever since. In 2015 it vanished completely, replaces by other Hibiki Expressions like Hibiki Harmony, which doesn’t carry an age statement.

In 2026, after an 11 year hiatus, Hibiki 12 Years Old has returned, this time as a global travel retail exclusive. According to parent company Suntory, the whisky has been “reimagined” by Chief Blender Shinji Fukuyo. The new blend includes malts from Yamazaki and Hakushu, along with grain whisky from Chita. Components were matured across American oak, Spanish oak, and Mizunara oak casks.

The final product remains the same strength (86 proof) as before. But there’s at least one noteworthy difference. Unlike earlier versions of Hibiki 12, no portions of the new-look blend were aged in umeshu (plum liqueur) casks.

Here’s a look at the new spirit alongside our original (if limited) coverage from 2009.

Hibiki 12 Years Old (2026) Review

This reimagined blend starts off light and floral on the nose, with rose petal, violet, honeysuckle, jasmine tea, grated nutmeg, Mizunara spice, and some barely-there strawberry shortcake. Later on, smaller whiffs of lychee, apple juice, and preserved pear add tart fruit, while touches of almond extract signal the grain whisky. A little vanilla showcases ex-bourbon cask influence, though it’s overall restrained, as is most of the oak; no single component (American, Spanish, or Japanese) punches far above the others.

First sips are moderately bready and grain-forward, accented with cocoa, lemon zest, and more spice. Next come toasted marshmallow and baking spice, alongside vanilla cookie and (subdued) candied ginger. Lychee, baked apple, and pear-flavored hard candy are discernible, though the palate is overall less fruity than the nose. Ginger and cinnamon highlight the midpalate, and cardamom builds from there through to the back palate and finish.

The finish brings the heaviest spice notes, with both Spanish and Mizunara oaks finally getting the chance to strut their stuff. Cardamom segues into delicate smoke and a bit of salted caramel. As per its reputation, Hibiki 12 does everything with a light touch, designed for sipping on a big rock to slowly unlock some of its sweeter and fruitier elements. (The marketing collateral recommends a hand-carved ice ball, but a large freezer cube will have to suffice for most.)

86 proof. B+ / $188 (700 ml) [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Hibiki 12 Years Old (2009) Review

This is a very easygoing, blended whiskey, pale gold in color and with a light, blonde-wood character that comes through strongly. Freshly brewed tea, a common characteristic in Japanese whiskeys, is huge on the palate, and the spirit eventually fades out with waves of grain, a light astringency, and some flowery notes. Very agreeable — though to be honest it reminds me a lot of 12-year Yamazaki, maybe with a touch more wood to it. CN

86 proof. B+ / $45 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
Jagermeister may be known for its impenetrably dark kräuterlikörs, but recently the company took things in an entirely new direction: Jagermeister Orange is exactly what it sounds like, an orange hued and flavored (and considerably lighter) version of its classic bitter sipper.

Per the company:

The liquid stays true to the brand’s heritage while introducing a more radiant, citrus-driven profile. Crafted in Germany using the same meticulous maceration process and attention to detail as the original, Jägermeister Orange owes its distinctive profile to the refinement with oils extracted from orange and mandarin peels. In fact, each bottle includes the oils of three Sicilian oranges delivering vibrant freshness and a modern taste experience at 33% abv.

Like all Jager expressions, Jager Orange is designed to be enjoyed ice cold as a shot, but it can also be used as a mixer in tall drinks. (Lemon-lime soda is suggested.)

Let’s give it a whirl.

Jagermeister Orange Review

The first transparent expression from Jagermeister, this looks nothing like the Jager you know and love, but more like an orange curacao. And on the nose, yes, some of the classic bitter-herbal notes of classic Jagermeister are present, but it’s really nothing like the original. Orange, naturally, dominates, a blend of juice and peel, lanced through with a spear of amaro. More traditional Jager-like notes of root beer, gentian, cloves, and spearmint peek out from around the edges — growing more insistent as it develops in glass.

The palate is equally a blend of the two hemispheres of this spirit’s brain. As with the nose, orange notes, quite juicy and sweet, dominate at first, but the more brooding, intense digestif qualities of Jagermeister come into focus in short order. Here they are not nearly as aggressive as on the nose, offering a more restrained character that is driven by clove and mint, only slightly bitter.

Curiously, the combination of bitterness and citrus gives the spirit a bit of a tiki vibe, and I increasingly wonder how it would fare as an alternative to standard triple sec in all manner of cocktails. Stay tuned.

66 proof.

A- / $23
